items.location: Limitations, "Model judges" (merged: skeptic critical; consistency reviewer wording)
items.problem: The main validity threat is understated. The paper argues that self-preference cannot favor any one condition, but the circularity is wider than that. Same-family agents drafted the skill. Versions 5 and 6 were built from these judges' comments. The editor prompt in every round, and seven of the ten held-out reader prompts, cast the judge as someone hunting for AI writing, which is what the skill targets. The held-out round is held out over briefs, not over judges. The wording is also inconsistent with the rest of the paper: "shuffled labels" (Sec. 4 says no labels), "reader lenses" and "model tier". "Hid labels" would also be inaccurate, because file paths showed the condition (see the Judges item).

DEVLOG sec. 13: v6 built from every judge comment in both panels. Recomputed mean Kendall tau on held-out rankings: editor-reader 0.78, editor-reader2 0.62, reader-reader2 0.55.
items.old_text: We shuffled labels, used two reader lenses, and in the held-out study added a judge running on a different model tier; we did not test judges from other model families or recruit enough human raters.
items.new_text: We replaced condition names with neutral labels (though file paths still showed them; Section~\ref{sec:eval}), shuffled the order of texts, used two judge roles (editor and genre reader), and in the held-out round added a judge running on another model of the same family; we did not test judges from other model families or recruit enough human raters. The circularity goes beyond self-preference: agents from the same family drafted the skill, versions~5 and~6 were built from these judges' comments, and the editor prompt in every round, like most reader prompts, cast the judge as someone watching for AI writing (``knows the research on AI-writing tells'', ``wary of AI-written work''), which is what the skill was built to remove. The held-out round is held out over briefs, not over judges, so our results show what judges from this family prefer. The two same-model judges also agreed with each other (mean Kendall $\tau$ 0.78) more than with the third judge (0.55--0.62).

items.location: Sec. 4 Evaluation, "Judges" paragraph, last sentence (skeptic)
items.problem: The unit of analysis isn't stated. Counts such as "47 of 48 judgments" suggest 48 independent observations, but the three judgments of a brief rate the same texts. The bootstrap intervals resample judgments, so they are too narrow, and the 15 pairwise tests per round get no multiple-comparison correction. The tests themselves correctly use per-brief means, and every reported result survives Holm correction, so stating this is all that's needed. The threshold is 0.025, not the skeptic's 0.023: v4 vs word list adjusts to 0.0234.
items.evidence: scripts/analyze.py: boot_ci resamples per-judgment rows; Friedman and Wilcoxon (zero_method='zsplit') run on per-brief mean ranks. Recomputed brief-level bootstrap: v4 [1.52, 2.38] (reported [1.62, 2.23]). Holm over analyze.py's 15 held-out p-values: v4 vs plain 0.006, v4 vs humanizer 0.009, Rebuild vs humanizer 0.009, v4 vs word list 0.0234, v6 vs word list 0.047, v4 vs Rebuild 0.085.
items.old_text: We report mean rank with bootstrap confidence intervals, a Friedman test across conditions on per-brief mean ranks, and pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
items.new_text: We report mean rank with bootstrap confidence intervals over judgments, a Friedman test across conditions on per-brief mean ranks, and pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on per-brief mean ranks, so the unit of every test is the brief (16 held-out), not the judgment (48). Judgments of one brief rate the same texts, and the two same-model judges agreed closely (mean Kendall $\tau$ 0.78), so the intervals understate uncertainty: resampling briefs instead widens version~4's held-out interval from [1.62, 2.23] to [1.52, 2.38]. Over the 15 held-out pairwise tests, Holm's correction keeps every comparison we report as significant below an adjusted $p$ of 0.025.

summary:
The four reviewers' findings came to 79 edits: 3 critical, 32 major and 44 minor. Overlapping items were merged into one edit each.

**The skeptic's three most important concerns, in plain words**
1. **The released version was picked using the test set.** Versions 4 and 6 were both frozen before the held-out briefs were written. The author then chose version 4 because it did better on those same briefs. The released version 7 was assembled after that and was never tested as a whole. So "the skill beat everything on held-out briefs" is somewhat flattering. The conclusion still holds, because version 6 also beat every baseline, but the paper has to say so.
2. **One model family did everything.** Same-family agents wrote the skill, produced every text and judged them. Versions 5 and 6 were tuned on those judges' comments. Most judges were told to hunt for AI writing, which is exactly what the skill hides. The held-out round tests new briefs, not new judges. So the results show what this model family likes, not what human readers like.
3. **The judging was not fully blind.** Judges opened the texts through file paths that contained the condition letter. My recheck found this is worse than the skeptic reported: 6 of 128 writing judgments name each text's condition letter (for example "T3 (L)"), and the coaching counselor labelled all six students' feedback by path.

**Verification.** I recomputed every numeric correction from eval/results using analyze.py, judges.py, the score files, the coaching files and the scripts. Where the local notes or full texts allowed, I also checked the citation claims, including Chakrabarty's 28%/20%/18%/17% and Karr's "Jr.".

All reviewer numbers held except these, which I changed:
- The skeptic said no writing judge named a condition. That is false (see concern 3).
- The skeptic's Holm threshold of 0.023 is really 0.0234, so the edit says "below 0.025".
- "Every text the skill wrote passed" is false for version 6 (its explain_6 text scored 35.6% on D1), so the edit names version 4.
- The skeptic's "15 humanizer skills" is 11.
- The coach feedback length is 2,263 by wc -w; the paper's 2,264 is not reproducible by either counting method.
- The "arithmetic-heavy" quote is about the version 6 Rebuild, which also runs on version 6's files. That makes it an overgeneralization rather than a misattribution, so I downgraded it to minor.

**Checks on the edit list**
- Every old_text occurs exactly once in main.tex or references.bib, and no two edits overlap.
- I applied all 79 edits to a scratch copy and compiled it: no undefined citations or references and no overfull boxes.
- The body still ends on page 8, so there is very little room for anything more.
- The merged abstract is 198 words, under ACL's 200-word limit.
- The new bib entries are one edit appended after the yale2026ai entry. Add real access dates to the two college-essay entries.

**Dropped**
- The scripts/figures.py change: it is not in main.tex. Its label fixes are still worth making by hand.
